title: Mayors on fiscal devolution: what it really means for growth, borrowing and fairness
label: 15 September 2026 · Fiscal devolution in England
summary: Mayors Howard Dawber (London deputy mayor) and Lord Houchen (Tees Valley mayor) explained how handing regions more control over money and taxes could speed up local projects, let areas borrow for infrastructure and change who decides on big planning schemes — but warned it’s not the same as full tax independence. They argued devolution helps growth if it gives stable, long-term income and protects basic services, while highlighting risks: unequal starting points between places, the need for sensible equalisation, borrowing caps, and the knock-on effects for local councils and skills.

speakers.label: Howard Dawber
speakers.name: Howard Dawber
speakers.role: Deputy Mayor of London for Business and Growth, London City Hall

glossary.definition: A group of local councils that join up to run big regional services together, often led by a directly elected mayor.
A specific kind of government grant paid to councils or combined authorities, named after the law that creates it.
A tax businesses pay on the buildings they use — like a property tax for shops and factories.
A charge on new development that a mayor can use to pay for local projects like transport or schools.
A system to smooth out differences so poorer places get more support and richer places give up some money.
The ability of a mayor or central government to take control of a big local planning decision from a council.

chapters.title: What fiscal devolution actually is
chapters.takeaway: Giving regions control of certain tax income or replacing many small grants with a single long-term grant can speed up local projects — but what’s on offer now isn’t the same as full tax independence.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. We’re talking about fiscal devolution — whether giving regions more control over money and taxes helps places grow.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Short answer: yes, if it's done right. Take Crossrail, the Elizabeth line: London had to fight for the funding route; if the mayor had had more fiscal levers up front we could've moved faster.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: I agree it helps, but be careful with words. The Government’s idea is often to replace lots of grants with one long grant — a Section 31 grant — not to hand over full control of a tax.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: That matters because a tax-based income — like a cut of income tax or keeping business rates — can be borrowed against, whereas grants are less secure for lenders.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: So what’s being offered now is more flexibility and longer-term certainty, which helps planning and investment, but it’s not the same as regions running their own HMRC.

chapters.title: Borrowing, caps and financial realities
chapters.takeaway: Mayors could borrow more if they had stable tax income, but existing caps, guarantees and central safeguards limit how far they can go.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Cookham
turns.text: You say tax income is more reliable than grants. But governments can change tax rules. Is it really safer for borrowing?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Officials are looking at smoothing tools — 'cap and collar' ideas — to blunt big swings. Also most mayoral deals already have a hard cap on borrowing.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Lenders look at the legal income covenant. If you can show a steady tax stream or retained business rates, markets are more willing to lend — as London did for Crossrail.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Cookham
turns.text: So banks lend because the income looks secure, often backed ultimately by central government strength, not just the local authority alone.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Exactly. That’s why some projects which are expected to lose money year-on-year — like subsidised bus networks — won’t be market-financeable anyway.

chapters.title: Which taxes make sense and how to be fair
chapters.takeaway: Income tax and business rates are sensible devolvable taxes because they grow with the economy and are traceable, but baseline equalisation and protection for basic services are essential.

turns.speaker: Lord Petitgas
turns.text: If you could choose, what taxes would you devolve or assign to regions?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Four tests: does the tax grow with the local economy, is it stable, can you see where it's raised, and can the public link it to local decisions. That points to income tax and business rates first.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: They’re the easiest to administer. But watch out: business rates can collapse in old industrial areas and create perverse incentives — local authorities might stop chasing big investors if they don’t benefit.

turns.speaker: Lord Prentis of Leeds
turns.text: How should equalisation work so poorer areas aren’t left behind?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Start neutral: everyone should be no worse off on day one. Lock a baseline for about ten years so places keep the upside from growth, while protecting core services from shocks.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: And politics will matter: places already behind will press for more transfers. You need a clear, fair mechanism or you’ll just recreate grant-style redistribution under another name.

chapters.title: Who should take decisions — mayors or councils?
chapters.takeaway: Mayors give a clear, visible point of accountability for big regional projects, but powers to override local councils — especially on planning — will create tensions that need careful rules and scrutiny.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: If you build regional powers into mayors, won’t that mean they end up dictating to councils, creating a democratic problem?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: In London we have a mayor and an assembly that scrutinises him; we also work closely with boroughs. For big, cross-boundary things — transport, big housing sites — city-level action often makes sense.

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Outside London, combined authorities were meant to be collegiate. But rules have shifted — more mayoral powers and fewer unanimous checks — so friction is likely when mayors can 'call in' planning decisions.

turns.speaker: Lord Razzall
turns.text: How clear is accountability between a mayor and a combined authority?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Legally it's clear if you read the statutes, but it's complex and not easy for the public to follow. Different places use different checks and scrutiny, so consistency would help.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: Is the mayor calling in planning a good move or likely to cause conflict?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: We’ve used call-in powers in London to keep a strategic view. It’s sensible if paired with transparent reasons and proper appeal routes so decisions aren't arbitrary.

chapters.title: Practical risks: capacity, reorganisation and local skills
chapters.takeaway: Devolution can empower places that plan well, but unequal starting points, limited local capacity, and uncertainty over reorganising councils mean support, training and smart equalisation will be needed.

turns.speaker: Lord Burns
turns.text: If we'd had these powers 25 years ago, would regional inequality be less now?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: Teesside would be different in some ways, but industrial decline could have still hit us. Devolution helps when paired with local assets and the right protections against shocks.

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: Different places have different starting capabilities. London is big, with lots of staff and institutions; smaller combined authorities will need time and support to build capacity.

turns.speaker: Baroness Alexander of Cleveden
turns.text: The Government paused local government reorganisation — does that stall devolution?

turns.speaker: Howard Dawber
turns.text: It shouldn’t stop giving more powers to existing mayoral areas. Reorg is an organisational question; devolution can proceed for places ready now.

turns.speaker: Lord Reid of Cardowan
turns.text: Do poorer places risk losing local skills to regions, or can devolution help grow local capability?

turns.speaker: Lord Houchen of High Leven
turns.text: It can do both. Devolution has helped Teesside pivot to big projects, using local industrial skills. But places need training, staff and long-term income to build capability.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both — we’ve heard practical benefits, important caveats on fairness, and clear notes on accountability and capacity.
